claims.text: Operating near an alloy's order-disorder transition enhances its structural and chemical stability.
Irradiation-induced ballistic mixing is enhanced near the order-disorder transition.
Ballistic mixing reduces chemical short-range order.
Reducing short-range order suppresses precipitation and limits grain coarsening.
As-deposited W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf refractory high-entropy-alloy thin films can have a nanocrystalline grain structure.
The as-deposited W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy contains intrinsic short-range order.
Approximately 1173 K is near the order-disorder transition temperature of the proposed alloy.
Approximately 800 K is sufficiently below the order-disorder transition temperature to provide a low-temperature comparison.
The high- and low-temperature groups will be processed under matched irradiation dose and environmental conditions.
Increasing temperature toward the order-disorder transition reduces the stability of short-range order.
Irradiation-induced atomic displacements mix the elements more effectively near the order-disorder transition.
Enhanced elemental mixing minimizes local chemical fluctuations that drive precipitation.
At temperatures well below the order-disorder transition, persistent short-range order promotes ordered-precipitate nucleation and consequent grain coarsening.
Treatment at 1173 K can preserve or refine the nanocrystalline grain structure of W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf films.
Near-transition treatment will produce less precipitation and grain coarsening than treatment at approximately 800 K.
Near-transition treatment will yield higher hardness than lower-temperature treatment.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies primarily to refractory high-entropy alloys whose service temperature is close to their order-disorder transition temperature.
Failure of the near-transition group to suppress precipitation and grain coarsening relative to the low-temperature group would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Thermal annealing and dual-beam irradiation are presented as interchangeable treatments, but the stated mechanism specifically requires irradiation-induced atomic displacements and ballistic mixing. An annealing-only comparison would not directly test that mechanism.
